title: Fainting (vasovagal syncope)
blurb: The most common emergency in the dental surgery: why patients faint, how to lie them flat and raise the legs, and how to know they've fully recovered.
question: A nervous 19-year-old watches the dentist pick up the local anaesthetic syringe. He goes pale and sweaty, says he feels sick and dizzy, then slumps in the chair. What is the most likely cause, and what is the immediate management?

teach.body: A vasovagal faint (syncope) is a brief loss of consciousness caused by a temporary drop in blood flow to the brain. It is the most common medical emergency in dental practice. Fear, pain, the sight of a needle or blood, heat, hunger and tiredness can over-stimulate the vagus nerve. The heart slows, blood vessels widen, blood pools in the legs and the blood pressure falls. Laid flat, the patient usually recovers quickly.

teach.h: A faint, from warning to recovery

items.label: Pale, clammy, sweating, yawning; dizzy, sick, blurred vision
Brief loss of consciousness; slow, weak pulse
Colour and consciousness return within moments
May feel tired or embarrassed; sit up slowly

teach.caption: Act on the warning signs: laying the patient back early can stop them losing consciousness at all.

root.label: Patient feels faint or faints
root.sub: Stop treatment, lay flat, raise the legs

children.label: Keep flat, monitor
children.sub: Sit up slowly once colour returns

children.edge: Slow to recover or not breathing normally
children.label: ABCDE, call 999

items: Stop treatment and remove instruments from the mouth.
Lay the patient flat: recline the dental chair fully and raise the legs.
Loosen tight clothing, reassure, and check the airway and breathing.
Keep them lying down until their colour returns and they feel well.
Sit them up slowly, in stages, and check they feel normal at each stage.
If they don't come round quickly, reassess with ABCDE, give oxygen and call 999.

teach.body: When a patient is upright, the heart has to pump blood uphill to the brain. Lying flat removes that climb, and raising the legs sends the blood that pooled in them back towards the heart. Blood flow to the brain recovers within moments. Sitting or standing a fainting patient keeps the brain short of blood, so never prop them upright or put their head between their knees. A heavily pregnant patient should be tilted onto her left side so the baby doesn't press on the large veins.

teach.caption: If a 'faint' doesn't recover quickly once the patient is flat, it may not be a faint.

teach.text: Don't sit the patient up as soon as they open their eyes. Sitting up too quickly is a common cause of a second faint. And if they don't recover quickly once flat, it isn't 'just a faint': reassess with ABCDE and think hypo, heart problem or seizure.

teach.body: Ask anxious patients if they have eaten, and recline them before injections. Raise the chair slowly at the end of treatment, because standing up quickly after lying back can cause a postural faint. After a faint, the dentist decides whether treatment continues, the episode is recorded in the notes, and the patient should not leave until fully recovered, ideally with someone. The same first aid applies to a colleague who feels faint: get them sitting or lying down, and don't let them carry on chairside.

items: Vasovagal syncope is the most common medical emergency in dental practice.
Signs: pale, sweaty, dizzy, nauseous, yawning; slow, weak pulse; brief loss of consciousness.
Stop, lay flat and raise the legs; loosen clothing; monitor airway and breathing.
Recovery is quick once flat; sit up gradually and confirm full recovery before they leave.
No quick recovery: ABCDE, oxygen, call 999; CPR if not breathing normally.

summary: You can now explain why a vasovagal faint happens, spot the warning signs, lay the patient flat with legs raised, manage their recovery safely, and recognise when a collapse is something more serious that needs ABCDE, 999 or CPR.

A.q: An anxious patient goes pale and sweaty when he sees the LA syringe, says he feels dizzy and sick, then slumps. He comes round quickly once the chair is laid flat. What is the most likely cause?
A.why: Pallor, sweating and dizziness triggered by anxiety, with quick recovery when flat, are classic features of a vasovagal faint.

whyNot.0: Anaphylaxis follows exposure to a trigger and causes swelling, wheeze or rash.
whyNot.2: A hypo causes shaking and confusion and doesn't recover just by lying flat.
whyNot.3: Stroke causes one-sided weakness and speech problems that persist.

A.q: A patient says she feels faint and looks pale and clammy. What is the immediate management?
options: Sit her up with her head between her knees
Walk her outside for some fresh air
Give her a glass of cold water
Lay her flat and raise her legs
A.why: Lying flat with legs raised restores blood flow to the brain and is the correct immediate management.

whyNot.0: Keeping the patient upright keeps the brain short of blood.
whyNot.1: Walking a fainting patient risks a fall and injury.
whyNot.2: A drink doesn't treat reduced blood flow to the brain and could be choked on.

A.q: Which is the most common medical emergency in dental practice?
A.why: Vasovagal syncope (fainting) is the most common medical emergency seen in the dental surgery.

whyNot.1: Cardiac arrest is rare in dental practice.
whyNot.2: Anaphylaxis is serious but much less common than fainting.
whyNot.3: Stroke can happen but is far less common than a faint.

B.q: Why does laying a fainting patient flat with the legs raised help?
options: It helps blood reach the brain
It slows the heart rate further
B.why: Lying flat removes the need to pump blood uphill, and raising the legs returns pooled blood, so the brain's blood supply recovers.

whyNot.1: Faster breathing isn't the aim; blood flow to the brain is the problem.
whyNot.2: The heart has already slowed in a faint; the aim is to improve circulation.
whyNot.3: Sweating stops as the patient recovers, but that's not why positioning works.

B.q: A patient comes round about a minute after fainting. What should happen next?
options: Restart the injection while he's calm
Keep flat, sit up in stages
B.why: He stays flat until his colour returns and he feels well, then sits up slowly in stages to avoid a second faint.

whyNot.0: Sitting up too quickly commonly causes a second faint.
whyNot.1: Treatment shouldn't restart until he has fully recovered and the dentist decides.
whyNot.3: Glucagon treats a severe hypo in a patient who can't swallow.

B.q: A patient has been laid flat with legs raised but hasn't regained consciousness after several minutes. What should you do?
options: Keep waiting, it's only a faint
Sit her up to help her wake
B.why: A faint recovers quickly once flat. Failure to recover suggests another cause, so reassess with ABCDE and call 999.

whyNot.0: Prolonged unconsciousness is not typical of a faint and needs urgent action.
whyNot.2: Sitting an unconscious patient up is dangerous and worsens blood flow to the brain.
whyNot.3: Nothing should be given by mouth to an unconscious patient.

C.q: Which of these is NOT a common trigger for a vasovagal faint?
C.why: A latex allergy causes an allergic reaction, possibly anaphylaxis, not a vasovagal faint.

whyNot.0: Anxiety is the classic trigger for a faint.
whyNot.1: The sight of a needle or blood often triggers fainting.
whyNot.2: Heat and hunger make fainting more likely.

C.q: During a long session, your colleague says she feels light-headed and looks pale. What is the best action?
options: Let her keep working if she sits
Have her lie down and get help
Give her a coffee and carry on
Send her home alone by car
C.why: A colleague who feels faint should be laid down safely and helped, and should not carry on chairside.

whyNot.0: Carrying on while faint risks her collapsing and harming the patient.
whyNot.2: Coffee doesn't treat a faint, and carrying on is unsafe.
whyNot.3: Driving while faint is dangerous; she needs to recover first.

C.q: Which sign suggests a vasovagal faint rather than cardiac arrest?
C.why: A faint recovers quickly once the patient is flat. In cardiac arrest there is no recovery and breathing is absent or abnormal.

whyNot.0: Absent or abnormal breathing in an unresponsive patient means cardiac arrest: start CPR.
whyNot.1: A grey or blue colour suggests a lack of oxygen, as in cardiac arrest.
whyNot.3: Briefly unresponsive is possible in a faint, but it alone doesn't tell them apart.

reteach.title: Pumping water uphill
reteach.question: Imagine a pump pushing water up a hill to a house. What happens if the pump slows down, and what is the quickest fix?

blocks.body: The heart is the pump, the brain is the house at the top of the hill. In a faint, fear makes the pump slow down and the pipes widen, so water stops reaching the house and the lights go out. You can't speed up the pump, but you can take away the hill: lay the patient flat so the brain is level with the heart, and lift the legs to send pooled blood back. The lights come back on within moments.

explain.body: A trigger such as fear or pain over-stimulates the vagus nerve. The heart slows and blood vessels widen, so blood pressure falls and the brain gets less blood.

test.q: What causes the loss of consciousness in a vasovagal faint?
options: A blocked artery in the brain
Brief drop in blood flow to the brain
test.why: A faint is a temporary drop in blood flow to the brain caused by a slow heart and widened blood vessels.

whyNot.0: A blocked artery in the brain causes a stroke.
whyNot.1: Low blood glucose is a hypo.
whyNot.2: Airway swelling is a feature of anaphylaxis.

explain.body: Pale, clammy, sweating, yawning, dizzy, nauseous, blurred vision, with a slow, weak pulse. Act now and the patient may not lose consciousness at all.

test.q: Which sign most suggests a patient is about to faint after an LA injection?
test.why: Pallor and sweating are the classic warning signs of a vasovagal faint.

whyNot.0: A faint makes the patient pale, not flushed.
whyNot.2: Swollen lips suggest an allergic reaction.
whyNot.3: Fruity breath suggests very high blood glucose.

explain.body: Stop treatment, recline the chair fully and raise the legs. Loosen tight clothing, reassure and check the airway and breathing.

test.q: A patient faints in the dental chair. What position should the chair be put into?
test.why: A fully reclined chair with the legs raised gets blood back to the brain fastest.

whyNot.0: Upright keeps the brain short of blood.
whyNot.2: Half reclined still leaves the head above the heart.
whyNot.3: Head-up makes blood flow to the brain worse.

explain.body: Keep the patient flat until their colour returns and they feel well, then sit them up slowly in stages. If they don't recover quickly, reassess with ABCDE, give oxygen and call 999.

test.q: Which action is most likely to cause a second faint after a patient comes round?
options: Raising their legs on the chair
test.why: Sitting up too soon lets blood pool in the legs again before the circulation has settled.
